meta.titre: Investment Demand: interest rates, expectations and government policy
meta.sous_theme: Determinants of private investment and the MEC

sections.contenu_markdown: Suppose that a cocoa processor in Douala thinks of buying a new machine and that a transport firm in Bamenda considers extra lorries. Each must decide whether the extra output will earn more than the machine or lorry costs, including the cost of the money borrowed to buy it. The same question, asked across the whole economy, gives the investment demand curve. Examiners ask you to explain the determinants of private investment and to say how a government might raise it. This course gives you the theory, a calculation method and a plan for evaluation.

items: Capital goods are man-made goods, such as machines and buildings, used to produce other goods.
The rate of interest is the price of borrowing money, and also the reward for lending it.
Depreciation is the fall in value of capital goods through wear and ageing.
Aggregate demand is total planned spending in the economy and includes consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.

sections.titre: Investment demand: the MEC, the interest rate and shifts of the curve
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Meaning of investment
In economics **investment** is spending on **new capital goods** (machines, buildings, equipment and increases in stocks) that add to productive capacity. It does **not** mean buying shares or saving money in a bank, which is financial investment. **Gross investment** is total spending on capital goods. **Net investment** is gross investment minus depreciation (replacement investment): $I_{net} = I_{gross} - \text{depreciation}$.

### Why investment demand falls as the interest rate rises
Keynes called the expected rate of return on an extra unit of capital the **marginal efficiency of capital (MEC)**. A firm compares it with the rate of interest, which is either the cost of borrowing or the return from lending its own funds instead (the opportunity cost). The rule is:

$$\text{invest if } \text{expected rate of return} > \text{rate of interest}$$

Firms rank projects from the highest to the lowest expected return. When the interest rate is high only the most profitable projects pass the test. When it falls, projects with lower returns become worth doing. So the **investment demand curve slopes downward** when the interest rate is on the vertical axis and the level of investment on the horizontal axis. A change in the interest rate is a **movement along** the curve.

### Shifts of the curve
Anything that changes the **expected returns** at each interest rate shifts the curve.

| Shift to the right (more investment) | Shift to the left (less investment) |
|---|---|
| Higher business confidence | Lower confidence, uncertainty |
| Expected rise in demand and income | Expected fall in demand |
| New technology | Higher taxes on company profits |
| Tax allowances or subsidies for investment | Higher prices of capital goods |
| Political stability and better infrastructure | Insecurity, poor roads and electricity |

### How strongly does investment respond to the interest rate?
Many economists argue that investment is **interest-inelastic**, especially in a slump: firms look mainly at expected demand and profit, so a cut in interest rates may do little unless confidence returns. The higher the uncertainty, the less the interest rate matters.

variantes.contenu_markdown: Explain at least four, each with a reason: the rate of interest and availability of credit; expected profit and expected demand (including the accelerator effect of rising output); business confidence and uncertainty; technology; taxes, subsidies and the cost of capital goods; and the stability of the economy, security and infrastructure. Good answers say whether each factor moves along the investment demand curve (interest rate) or shifts it (the others).

variantes.nom: How a government can increase investment
variantes.quand_utiliser: A 'how can the government...' question with evaluation
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Lower interest rates** or easier credit, which move firms down the investment demand curve.
- **Tax incentives**: lower company tax, investment allowances, subsidies.
- **Public investment** in roads, electricity and ports, which makes private projects more profitable.
- **A stable environment**: low inflation, security, clear rules, less bureaucracy, to raise confidence.
- **Education and training**, and measures to attract foreign investors.

Evaluation: lower interest rates may not work if confidence is low, tax incentives reduce government revenue, government borrowing may raise interest rates and crowd out private firms, and effects take time.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Short calculation questions on whether to invest
variantes.contenu_markdown: If a machine costs 1,000,000 FCFA and is expected to add 150,000 FCFA a year to net revenue, the expected annual rate of return is $150{,}000 \div 1{,}000{,}000 = 15\%$. This simple measure assumes that the annual return is constant. The firm invests if 15% exceeds the interest rate.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A firm has five possible projects. Each has an expected annual rate of return and a cost.

| Project | Expected return (%) | Cost (million FCFA) |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 22 | 30 |
| P2 | 17 | 45 |
| P3 | 13 | 60 |
| P4 | 9 | 35 |
| P5 | 6 | 50 |

(a) Find the investment that the firm wants at interest rates of 15%, 10% and 4%.
(b) Explain what the results show about the shape of the investment demand curve.
(c) Business confidence falls and every expected return is 5 percentage points lower. Find the investment at an interest rate of 10% and name the type of change.

etapes.justification: A project is worth doing only when its expected return exceeds the interest rate.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Invest in project $j$ if return $>$ interest rate.

etapes.justification: Only projects with returns above 15% pass.

etapes.resultat_markdown: At 10%: P1, P2 and P3 (13%): 30 + 45 + 60 = **135 million**. At 4%: all five projects: 30 + 45 + 60 + 35 + 50 = **220 million**.

etapes.justification: Investment rises as the interest rate falls.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The pairs (15%, 75), (10%, 135) and (4%, 220) give a downward-sloping curve, a staircase for a few projects and a smooth curve for many.

etapes.justification: Lower expected returns shift the curve because they change what happens at every interest rate.
etapes.resultat_markdown: New returns: 17%, 12%, 8%, 4%, 1%. At 10%, only P1 and P2 pass: 30 + 45 = **75 million**, down from 135. The curve has **shifted to the left**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Investment is 75 million FCFA at 15%, 135 million at 10% and 220 million at 4%. (b) The investment demand curve slopes downward because lower interest rates make more projects worthwhile. (c) After the 5-point fall in expected returns, investment at 10% is only 75 million FCFA, a leftward shift of the curve caused by lower confidence, not by a change in the interest rate.

items.erreur_markdown: Defining investment as buying shares or putting money in a savings account.
items.pourquoi_faux: In economics investment means spending on capital goods that add to productive capacity. Buying shares transfers ownership.
items.correction_markdown: Define investment as spending on new capital goods, and say that financial investment is a different thing.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing a change in the interest rate as a shift of the investment demand curve.
items.pourquoi_faux: The interest rate is on the axis of the diagram, so its change causes a movement along the curve.
items.correction_markdown: Use movement along the curve for the interest rate and a shift for expectations, taxes, technology or confidence.

items.erreur_markdown: "A cut in interest rates always raises investment."
items.pourquoi_faux: If firms expect weak demand or are uncertain, they will not invest even at low rates. Investment is often interest-inelastic.
items.correction_markdown: Say that a cut in interest rates helps only when expected returns are high enough, and mention confidence.

items.pourquoi_faux: Gross investment includes replacement of worn-out capital. Only net investment increases the capital stock.
items.correction_markdown: Compute net investment as gross investment minus depreciation.

items.erreur_markdown: Giving a list of government measures without any evaluation.
items.pourquoi_faux: A 'how' question for 10 marks rewards explanation, and a good answer also considers costs and limits.
items.correction_markdown: Explain how each measure raises investment and add one limit, for example crowding out or time lags.

items.enonce_markdown:
In an economy gross investment in a year is 120 billion FCFA and depreciation of the capital stock is 45 billion FCFA.

(a) Calculate net investment.
(b) State what has happened to the capital stock.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Net investment = gross investment - depreciation = 120 - 45 = **75 billion FCFA**.

(b) Net investment is positive, so **the capital stock has increased** by 75 billion FCFA, and productive capacity has grown.

items.enonce_markdown:
A bakery can buy an oven for 2,400,000 FCFA. The oven is expected to add 336,000 FCFA a year to net revenue (assume this is constant).

(a) Calculate the expected annual rate of return.
(b) Decide whether the bakery should buy the oven when the interest rate is 12% and when it is 16%.
(c) State one non-interest factor that could change the decision.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 336,000 divided by 2,400,000 = 0.14, so the expected rate of return is **14%**.

(b) At 12%, the return of 14% is higher than the cost of funds, so **buy**. At 16%, the return is lower, so **do not buy**.

(c) Any one of: a change in expected demand for bread, new technology, taxes on profit, or the confidence of the owner. These alter the expected return, not the interest rate.

items.enonce_markdown: Evaluate the view that cutting the interest rate is the most effective way for a government to increase private investment.
items.solution_markdown:
Award marks for the following points:

- **For:** lower rates reduce the cost of borrowing and make more projects profitable, so firms move down the investment demand curve; they also reduce the opportunity cost of using own funds.
- **Against:** investment depends strongly on expected demand and confidence, so in a slump investment may respond little (interest-inelastic); banks may not lend; the effect has a time lag.
- **Other measures:** tax incentives, public investment in infrastructure, security and stability, and training raise expected returns and shift the curve, which may achieve more than a movement along it.
- **Judgement:** **a cut in rates helps when confidence and expected demand are already good; otherwise measures that raise expected returns are more effective**, so the best policy is usually a combination.

items_markdown: Investment is spending on new capital goods; net investment = gross investment - depreciation.
A firm invests when the expected rate of return (MEC) exceeds the interest rate, so investment demand slopes downward against the interest rate.
A change in the interest rate is a movement along the curve; changes in expected profit, confidence, technology, taxes or demand shift it.
Investment is often interest-inelastic because expectations and uncertainty matter more than the cost of borrowing.
Government can raise investment through lower interest rates, tax incentives, infrastructure, stability and training, but must weigh cost, crowding out and time lags.
